To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the convolution method for optical microprobe spectroscopy is valid, and that it can be used to obtain information about material properties in the microprobe volume.

(i) the convolution procedure is valid for all cases in which there is significant absorption of light within the microprobe volume, (ii) the convolution procedure can be applied to both Raman and luminescence spectroscopies, (iii) the convolution procedure gives good agreement with test experiments on alumins and single crystals, and (iv) the method can be used to determine the composition and strain in a material using the microprobe
the convolution method is applicable to a wide range of microprobe spectroscopic measurements and that it provides an accurate means for interpreting such measurements.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of optical microprobe spectroscopy as a tool for the study of materials properties, and with the development of the theory necessary for the correct use of this technique.
the development of new techniques and instruments for the study of the structure and properties of materials on the microscopic scale, using optical spectroscopic methods.
the development and application of Raman microprobe spectroscopy to the analysis of materials.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the convolution procedure, as applied to the data presented here, provides a good description of the data, although the interpretation of the convolution is not unique and is not necessarily correct.

, for the case in which the optical microprobe response function can be approximated by a Gaussian function, and for the case inwhich the material shows significant optical absorption, it is necessary, in order to obtain an accurate interpretation of optical microprobe spectra, to convolute the variation of material properties within the microprobe with the optical microprobe function.
the convolution procedure, when applied to optical microprobe experiments, is a useful tool that can be used to interpret the results of many experiments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the convolution method is a powerful tool for extracting quantitative material property variation information from the observed optical spectra.
the optical microprobe is a powerful tool for the study of material properties that vary on a scale comparable with the optical penetration depth.
, for the first time, it is now possible to obtain quantitative measurements of composition or strain variations in materials with a resolution of 1 μm and an accuracy of 0.1%.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the optical microprobe can be used as a tool to measure the spatial variation of material properties, provided that the material property variation is not correlated to the optical absorption.

, when the material is strongly absorbing, the response function is not simply the spatial intensity profile of the microprobe, but rather the spatial intensity profile convoluted with the spatial variation of the material property.
, in order to interpret optical spectroscopic data from microprobe measurements of composition or strain, one should convolute the material properties with the microprobe response function.
